description: A rough, hairy, branched annual herb 20-60 cm tall that often creeps or sprawls and roots at the lower nodes. It has narrow lanceolate leaves in opposite pairs and small white daisy-like flower heads borne on short stalks in the leaf axils. Crushed stems stain the skin blackish.
cultural_significance: The name Kesharaja means 'king of hair', and it is the best-known Ayurvedic hair herb, a base of many traditional hair oils. It is also considered a Rasayana for the liver. It is not a Vedic-era plant by name; it is prominent in later Nighantus and folk traditions.
habitat: Moist ground, paddy-field margins, ditch banks, wet waste ground and lawns across warm tropical and subtropical regions; often grows as a weed.

uses.title: Hair fall and scalp care
uses.detail: Described as Keshya (beneficial for hair); the herb is cooked in sesame or coconut oil and traditionally massaged into the scalp to support hair growth and delay greying.

uses.title: Liver support and jaundice
uses.detail: Whole-plant juice or decoction is traditionally used in liver complaints and jaundice, and the herb is regarded as a hepatic Rasayana.

uses.title: Skin disorders and wounds
uses.detail: Fresh leaf paste is traditionally applied to wounds, itching and skin eruptions, and the juice is used for fungal-type skin complaints.

uses.title: Respiratory complaints
uses.detail: Leaf juice with honey is traditionally given in cough and breathing difficulty, and it is described as Kaphahara.

uses.title: Liver and hair research
uses.detail: Wedelolactone-rich extracts of Eclipta have been studied in animal and laboratory work for liver protection and hair growth; human evidence is limited and preliminary.

preparations.name: Bhringaraja taila (medicated hair oil)
preparations.method: Fresh herb juice cooked with sesame or coconut oil and supporting herbs by the classical taila method.
preparations.note: Applied to the scalp; a very common traditional hair oil.

preparations.name: Swarasa (fresh juice)
preparations.method: Crush the fresh herb and press out the juice; traditionally taken with honey.
preparations.note: Small quantities only; practitioner guidance advised.

preparations.name: Churna (dried powder)
preparations.method: Shade-dry the herb and grind to a fine powder; taken with warm water, honey or milk, or mixed with water as a hair mask.
preparations.note: Used internally as a tonic and externally on the scalp.

preparations.name: Leaf paste for external use
preparations.method: Grind fresh leaves into a paste and apply to minor wounds or skin patches.
preparations.note: Patch-test first; avoid deep or infected wounds.

precautions: Taken internally it may cause loose stools or stomach upset in some people. Scalp application can cause irritation or allergy in sensitive skin, so patch-test first; people allergic to daisy-family plants (Asteraceae) should take care. It may affect blood sugar and liver enzyme tests, so people on diabetes or liver-affecting medicines should consult a doctor. Avoid medicinal use in pregnancy and breastfeeding unless advised by a practitioner.

cultivation.climate: Warm, humid tropical to subtropical; frost-tender
cultivation.soil: Moist loamy or clayey soil, pH 5.5-7.5
cultivation.propagation: Seeds sown in the monsoon, or stem cuttings that root at the nodes
cultivation.harvest: Cut the whole herb at flowering, about 3-4 months after sowing, and use fresh or shade-dry

conservation_status: Not threatened; a common weed across the tropics, though wild collection for the hair-oil trade is heavy.
fun_fact: If you crush a fresh stem and rub it on the skin, it leaves a blackish stain, which is one reason it has long been linked in folk practice to darkening hair and used as a natural tattoo and hair dye ingredient.

regions.name: Tamil Nadu Plains
regions.note: Known as Karisalankanni; wet ground and field margins

regions.name: Thailand & Indochina
regions.note: Wet waste ground and rice-field edges

regions.name: Southern China
regions.note: Used in Chinese herbal medicine as Han Lian Cao
